newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-LVMH move threatens to delay Guinness deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-LVMH move threatens to delay Guinness deal.

text.p: A proposed 23 billion pound ($37.5 billion) merger between Britain's Grand Metropolitan Plc and drinks group Guinness Plc could be held up by the "spoiling tactics" of French drinks and luxury goods company LVMH, analysts said on Wednesday.

Shares in Guinness and GrandMet fell as LVMH, which holds an estimated 14.2 percent stake in Guinness, said it would exercise its option to buy Guinness out of all their joint venture companies if the latter went ahead with its merger with GrandMet.

LVMH, makers of France's Moet & Chandon champagne and Hennessy cognacs, said it believed the merger would create a "control event" that would allow it to exercise its option to buy Guinness' interests in the joint ventures at their net asset value, although Guinness disputed this.

"I think it will delay and disrupt the deal with lengthy legal proceedings in prospect and the chances of it going ahead in its current form are now much reduced," said Charles Winston, analyst at HSBC James Capel.
Guinness shares were down 15 pence at 581, while GrandMet was down 15-1/2, also at 581, by 1500 GMT.
A spokesman for Guinness, famous for its stout and leading whisky brands such as Johnnie Walker, said the company is confident its timetable for the merger would be unaffected by the LVMH decision.
"The timetable is put at three to eight months depending on whether the regulatory authorities grant their approval straight away," he said.
If the United States and European authorities let it through, then the merger could be consummated in three months, but if they chose to investigate it further it could be eight months, he said.
The merger already faces opposition from drinks and entertainment group Seagram, which claims the union would create anti-trust problems in the United States and Europe.

"Clearly Guinness believes they have structured the deal in such a way that it does not constitute a change of ownership and LVMH disagree, but any legal dispute could delay the merger," said Dermott Carr, analyst at Nikko.
Corporate lawyers at Guinness and GrandMet have pored over an agreement signed between Guinness and LVMH in 1994 to make sure it was not contravened by the terms of the merger.

A 1994 agreement provided that if there was a change in the ownership of Guinness then LVMH would have the right to buy, at net asset value, Guinness' interests in all their joint ventures and to keep exclusive distribution on rights on Guinness brands for at least 10 years in those markets.

LVMH also has the option to repurchase the 34 percent stake in Moet Hennessy owned by Guinness at a discounted price if this so-called "control event" is triggered. In January 1994, Guinness paid 902 million pounds for the stake in Moet Hennessey, which chipped in 113 million pounds to its 1996 full year profits.
"We are confident that it won't be triggered. Guinness is not being taken over, it is a merger," the Guinness spokesman said.
The proposed deal is technically structured as a takeover of GrandMet by Guinness, although the latter is slightly smaller in terms of market value.

Guinness shareholders would retain their shares in Guinness which would be renamed GMG Brands under the proposals, while GrandMet shareholders would get one GMG share for every one GrandMet share. GrandMet shares would be delisted.
GrandMet stuck by its merger partner, saying LVMH's threat did not affect their merger plans.
"Clearly the issue was looked at ahead of the merger announcement and we are confident that it will not affect in any way our proposed merger," said a GrandMet spokesman. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
